## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Chapter overview**
- A new series of prophecies starts here and runs to ch. 19, after the vision of chs. 8–11. (Ellicott)
- The chapter has two sign-acts: packing for exile (vv. 1–16) and eating with trembling (vv. 17–20). Then come two answers to scoffing sayings (vv. 21–28). (MHC; Clarke)
- John B. Taylor, quoted by Guzik, calls chs. 12–24 "objections to judgment," raised only so they can be knocked down. (EW)
- Pulpit thinks these signs were aimed at prophecies of quick deliverance that were going around both in Jerusalem and among the exiles. (Pulpit)
- Some older writers date these chapters to Zedekiah's sixth year, about five years before the siege. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-1.htm; Haydock)

**v. 1**
- Pulpit says this formula ("the word of the LORD came to me") appears here for the first time in Ezekiel and comes back repeatedly in this chapter. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-1.htm)
- Matthew Henry notes that the glory-vision had left, yet God's word still came to the prophet. (MHC)

**v. 2**
- Israel had the word of God, the priesthood, the temple and the prophets. They could have seen and heard, but they would not. (EW)
- This is the deliberate refusal to see that Scripture often describes. That is why God gave a sign they could not shut their eyes to. (Ellicott)
- JFB calls it a fulfilment of Deut 29:4. Their blindness comes from perversity, not inability. Ezekiel needed reminding of this so the poor response wouldn't discourage him. (JFB)
- Bible.org traces the theme through Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the Gospels. (Bible.org)
- Henry says God speaks to them in signs "as deaf people are taught." Ministers must adapt to their hearers' stubbornness, not just their weakness. (MHC)
- One older note links it to idolaters becoming like their idols (Ps 115). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/12-10.html)

**v. 3**
- Ezekiel was already an exile in Babylon. He acts out exile again to warn that those still in Jerusalem would soon join him. (EW)
- Guzik: false prophets were promising rescue from Babylon, and Jeremiah and Ezekiel opposed them. (EW)
- Bible.org: "in their sight" is repeated as a wordplay on their blindness, and "perhaps they will understand" is literally "perhaps they will see." (Bible.org)
- Calvin: "perhaps" shows how hard the people were. Preachers must keep going even when they see no results. (Calvin)

**v. 4**
- Ezekiel plays an exile, re-enacting a scene the exiles had lived through. (Feinberg, quoted in EW)
- Henry draws an application: hold this world loosely, since "we have here no continuing city." (MHC)

**v. 5**
- The wall was probably sun-dried brick, so it was easy to dig through. Coming and going through the wall suggests stealth. (Ellicott)
- It pictures a desperate escape from a besieged city. (Feinberg, quoted in EW)
- It foreshadows Zedekiah escaping through a breach (2 Kgs 25:4; Jer 39). (PA1; Clarke)

**v. 6**
- The Hebrew word for "twilight/dusk" means dark. It occurs only here, in v. 12 and in Gen 15:17. (Ellicott)
- Covering the face may be a sign of grief, but here it is mainly prophetic. (Ellicott)
- Barnes: mourning, and also a hint of Zedekiah's blindness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/12-6.html)
- Clarke speculates that Zedekiah might be carried with a cloth over his wounded eyes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/12-6.html)
- Calvin: frightened people veil their faces, and someone fleeing does not look down. (Calvin)
- Haydock: it points to Zedekiah's blindness or to an attempted disguise; criminals' faces were also covered (Esther 7). (Haydock)

**v. 7**
- Each time, Ezekiel did exactly what he was told. His actions and his words together carried the warning. (EW)

**v. 8**
- "In the morning" implies the sign was really performed, because God's message answers the people's question. (Ellicott)
- It suggests the explanation came the next day. (PA1)

**v. 9**
- The strange behaviour was meant to provoke the question "What are you doing?" (EW)
- Calvin and Keil both note that calling them a "rebellious house" again shows the question was not a sincere one. Calvin thinks they were mocking. (Calvin; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-16.htm)
- TGC: they physically saw him but remained spiritually clueless. (TGC)

**v. 10**
- "Burden" means a prophecy of woe. Ezekiel carrying his load pictured the weight of disaster coming on the king and people. (Barnes, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-12.htm)
- Coffman compares Nahum's "burden of Nineveh." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/12-10.html)
- The "prince" is Zedekiah. Guzik says Ezekiel never calls him king because the true king, Jehoiachin, was already in Babylon. (EW)
- Keil also says the prince is Zedekiah, not Jehoiachin, and translates the phrase as "the prince is this burden." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-16.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-12.htm)

**v. 11**
- On the phrase "I am your sign": what Ezekiel does among the exiles will soon happen in Jerusalem. (Pulpit)
- The sign was also for the exiles, whose hopes rested on the holy city staying safe. (Ellicott)
- JFB adds that it warned the exiles at the Chebar against hoping to return to a Jerusalem that was still standing. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-1.htm)

**v. 12**
- Zedekiah fled by night, was captured near Jericho, saw his sons killed at Riblah, and was blinded. (https://biblehub.com/study/ezekiel/12-12.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/12-10.html)
- Poole: he was probably disguised as a servant. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-12.htm)
- Henry: "God's judgments can turn a prince into a porter." (MHC)
- Calvin: it was shameful for a king to hide his face out of distrust of anyone he might meet. (Calvin)
- Keil: his attendants would have broken through the wall for him. The covered face is not in the historical accounts but is not unlikely as a sign of shame. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-12.htm)

**v. 13**
- The net is God's. God fought against Jerusalem, and God makes sure the king is caught (compare Hos 7:12). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-13.htm)
- God planned the capture and carried it out through Babylon's army. (Bible.org)
- On "he will not see it": Zedekiah saw Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, but he was blinded there, so he never saw Babylon even though he died there. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/ezekiel-12.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/12-10.html)
- Calvin dwells on how wretched his final imprisonment was. (Calvin)

**v. 14**
- Judah's people were not only taken to Babylon but scattered. After Gedaliah was murdered, the remnant fled to Egypt (Jer 41–43). (Ellicott)

**v. 15**
- "They shall know that I am the LORD" explains why God allowed such judgment: in the end, to make himself known, even through his judgments. (EW)

**v. 16**
- The survivors would confess their sins among the nations. This would show the nations that God was punishing sin, not failing to protect his people. (Ellicott; Keil at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-16.htm)
- JFB: the survivors would both turn from idols themselves and show God's justice to the Gentiles. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/12-16.htm)
- Poole gives three options: they tell of their sins, their misery speaks for itself, or their behaviour in exile shows God was just. (same page)
- Henry: the scattering of sinners leads to the scattering of penitents who honour God elsewhere. (MHC)

**vv. 17–18**
- A second sign: the terror of the siege. (EW; PA2)
- Block, quoted by Guzik: eating and drinking is life at its most basic, and the trembling announces that all is not well. (EW)
- Wiersbe, quoted by Guzik: every meal might be their last. (EW)
- Pulpit: the focus is the fear of the besieged, not the scarcity of food as in ch. 4. (Pulpit)
- Precept Austin compares ch. 4 and the coming 18-month siege. (PA2)
- Henry's application, cited by Precept Austin: preachers warning of ruin must speak "feelingly." (PA2)

**vv. 19–20**
- The land would be emptied of its fruitfulness because of their violence. What they did to others comes back on them. (Alexander, quoted in EW)

**v. 21**
- The fourth of five "word of the LORD" messages in this chapter. (PA2)

**v. 22**
- The saying meant that life would go on as before and the prophecies of doom would never happen. (EW)
- Feinberg, quoted by Guzik: the delay was God's mercy, and they turned it into an argument against his word. (EW)
- Ellicott: "in the land of Israel" points to people still in Judah who thought they would never be taken away. (Ellicott)
- Clarke: these were scoffers who took the delay of punishment as permission to sin. (Clarke)

**v. 23**
- Ezekiel answers their proverb with a counter-proverb. (Pulpit at https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/12-23.htm)
- Block, quoted by Guzik: "every vision" has not failed; "every vision" is about to be fulfilled. (EW)
- Ellicott: "effect" means "accomplishment." (Ellicott)
- Pulpit links this to "at hand" sayings in Matt 3:2 and 4:17 and in Rom 13:11. A true prophet always has a near fulfilment, which can also point to a later, fuller one. (Pulpit)

**v. 24**
- "Divination" suggests mechanical methods such as lots or arrows. Taylor, quoted by Guzik, says the term carries disapproval. (EW)
- Calvin compares Noah, who feared a judgment he could not yet see (Heb 11:7). (Calvin)

**v. 25**
- Whenever God speaks, the result must follow (Isa 55:11). (JFB)
- Calvin: a thousand years are as a day to God, but here God sets the time "after the manner of men." Those then alive would see it happen. (Calvin)
- Clarke: the mockers themselves would live to feel it. (Clarke)

**vv. 26–27**
- The objection changes slightly. These people accept that Ezekiel is a true seer but put the fulfilment far in the future. (Pulpit)
- Guzik: this is the heart's favourite way to put off repentance. (EW)
- Henry's paraphrase, cited by Precept Austin: "we may die in honor and peace before these troubles come." (PA2)
- Precept Austin connects this to the scoffers of 2 Pet 3. (PA2)

**v. 28**
- Clarke: God had waited to be gracious; they abused his mercy, and the wrath held back so long now broke out. (Clarke)
- Henry, cited by Precept Austin: "the longer the bow has been in the drawing the deeper shall the arrow pierce." (PA2)
- Application: don't treat God's patience as proof the warning will never come true. (EW)

---

## 2. Where Protestant writers differ

I found no sharp disagreement between denominations in this chapter. Two smaller differences came up:

**v. 2: the cause of their blindness**
- Clarke (Methodist): they are not lost for lack of grace. No one is lost because they lacked enough grace to be saved, only because they misused it. (Clarke)
- Calvin (Reformed) also puts the blame on their stubbornness: they "stupified themselves," and hypocrites cannot claim ignorance as an excuse. But he adds that the causes of God's judgments are not always visible, since sometimes a whole nation is blinded for reasons hidden from us. (Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-12.html)
- So both blame the people. Clarke uses the verse against the idea that grace was insufficient, while Calvin leaves room for God's hidden purposes.

**vv. 3–7: did Ezekiel actually do this?**
- JFB says Ezekiel was carried in spirit to Jerusalem and performed the acts in vision, not physically. (JFB)
- Ellicott argues that "in the morning" (v. 8) shows the action was really performed. (Ellicott)
- Keil, Pulpit and Precept Austin also treat it as a public act. Pulpit pictures Ezekiel crouching in terror in v. 18. (Pulpit; PA1)

---

## 3. Other views

**Modern critical dating (vv. 12–13)**
- Pulpit mentions scholars who treat predictions as written after the events. They conclude that this section was written after Jerusalem fell. Pulpit rejects that view. (Pulpit)

**Josephus and the apparent contradiction (v. 13)**
- Josephus says Ezekiel's prophecy was sent to Jerusalem. Zedekiah thought it contradicted Jeremiah, who said he would see the king of Babylon, so he refused to believe either prophet. (Pulpit; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/ezekiel-12.html)
- Pulpit doubts Josephus had any source beyond the two prophetic books. (Pulpit)

**Catholic (Haydock, drawing on Calmet, Theodoret and Challoner)**
- v. 6: the Douay text says the prince "shall be carried on shoulders." The covered face stands for Zedekiah's blindness or his disguise. (Haydock)
- v. 10: Theodoret says the prophecy was sent to Jerusalem to back up Jeremiah's warnings and encourage the exiles. "Israel" may include people from the ten tribes who had moved there. (Haydock)
- v. 13: Zedekiah was blinded, put in a cage "like a wild beast," and taken to Babylon. Haydock answers Thomas Paine's claim that this contradicts Jeremiah: the events showed both prophets were right. (Haydock)
- v. 22: the people used God's patience as an excuse to sin more. If a prophecy came true they called it chance, and if it was conditional they called it an excuse. Haydock compares heretics who deny the general judgment. (Haydock)
